# Introduction

Anderson and Gerbing (1988) explain how researchers can use SEM to test theories and study the relationships between different concepts.
The main idea of the article is the two-step approach.
First, researchers check if the measurement model is working well.
Then, they test the structural model to see how the concepts are related.

The reason for separating these steps is because measurement problems and relationship problems are not always the same.
If the measures are not working good, the results about the relationships can also be confusing.
So, researchers should first check the measures before explaining the results from the structural model.

# Background

SEM uses ideas from factor analysis and regression or path analysis.
A latent construct is something that researchers cannot see or measure directly, so they use several observed indicators to measure it.
For example, Salesforce adoption can be measured by looking at if employees log in, update records, document their activities, and follow the CRM process.

The measurement model looks at how the indicators measure the latent constructs.
The structural model looks at how the different constructs are related based on the theory.
These two parts are connected, but they are used for answer different questions.

# Exploratory Versus Confirmatory Analyses

Exploratory analysis is used when the researcher is not sure how many factors are in the data.
It helps researchers look for possible patterns.
Confirmatory analysis starts with a model that is already based on theory.
The researcher then checks if the data support this model.

The article says exploratory and confirmatory analysis are not always completely separate.
A researcher can start with a theory, find some problems, and make a few changes.
But if the researcher changes the model many times using the same data, the result may fit only that sample.
It is better to test the final model with another sample if this is possible.

This is important because a model can look good just because it was changed many times for the current data.
A new sample can help researchers know if the model also works for the larger population.

# Complementary Approaches for Theory Testing Versus Predictive Application

The authors explain that SEM can be used for different purposes.
One purpose is testing and developing theories.
Another purpose is predicting outcomes.
These purposes can require different methods.

For theory testing, full-information methods such as maximum likelihood (ML) and generalized least squares (GLS) can be useful.
These methods include measurement error and give information about the overall model fit.
PLS can be useful when the researcher mainly cares about prediction and explaining variance.

The authors do not say one method is always the best.
The method should depend on what the research is trying to do.
ML is more connected with theory testing, while PLS can be useful for prediction when the theory is not very developed.

# Estimation Methods

Maximum likelihood is one important method in SEM.
When its assumptions are reasonable, ML can give consistent and efficient estimates.
It also allows researchers to test individual parameters and the overall model fit.

The article also talks about problems when the data is not normally distributed.
Non-normal data can affect standard errors and chi-square tests.
The parameter estimates may still be okay sometimes, but the fit tests can be less reliable.

Because of this, researchers need to think about their data before choosing an estimation method.
Estimation is not only a computer option.
It can affect the conclusions of the study, especially when the sample is small or the data has unusual distribution.

# Confirmatory Measurement Model

The confirmatory measurement model explains which observed indicators belong to each latent construct.
At this stage, the constructs can be related to each other, but the researcher is not yet testing the main directional paths in the theory.

The measurement model helps researchers check construct validity.
A good model should have useful indicators, acceptable fit, and a meaning that makes sense.
The authors prefer using several indicators for each construct because one indicator cannot show much about measurement error.

For example, Salesforce adoption could include several indicators, such as login frequency, record updates, and documentation timeliness.
These indicators should measure the same general adoption idea instead of being unrelated work behaviors.

# Need for Unidimensional Measurement

Unidimensionality means that a group of indicators mainly measures one construct.
If the items are supposed to measure one construct but actually measure several different ideas, the meaning of the construct becomes unclear.

Internal consistency looks at how indicators within the same construct are related.
External consistency looks at how the construct behaves with other constructs.
Both ideas are useful for understanding if the measurement is working.

For example, items for Salesforce adoption should be connected to CRM usage.
They should not also include job satisfaction or general computer skill unless the theory says these ideas belong together.
Otherwise, the construct may not have a clear meaning.

# Specification

Model specification means deciding which indicators measure which constructs and which relationships should be included.
These decisions should come from theory, past research, and the meaning of the questions.
Researchers should not choose paths only because they make the model fit better.

The article recommends multiple indicators, but it also discusses single indicators and constructs with only two indicators.
These situations can make the model harder to estimate.
Researchers need to check if the model is identified and if there is enough information to estimate it.

Correlated measurement errors should also be used carefully.
Sometimes two errors may be related because the questions have similar wording or use the same method.
But researchers should not add correlated errors only because the fit becomes better.
There should be a reasonable explanation for the change.

# Assessment of Fit

After estimating the measurement model, researchers need to see if it fits the data.
The article discusses chi-square, fit indexes, residuals, and model comparisons.

Chi-square is useful, but it can be affected by the sample size.
In a large sample, even a small difference between the model and the data can become significant.
Because of this, researchers should not use chi-square alone.
They should also look at other fit information, residuals, sample size, and the theory behind the model.

Convergent validity is supported when indicators for the same construct have strong relationships.
Discriminant validity means that different constructs are not measuring the exact same thing.
These checks should happen before the researcher explains the structural paths.

# Respecification

Sometimes the first measurement model does not fit well.
Researchers may need to respecify it by removing a weak indicator, correcting an indicator assignment, or adding a relationship that has a clear theory reason.

The authors warn that respecification should not become a search for the best number only.
If researchers make many changes without a theory reason, the final model may fit the current sample but not work with another sample.

Improper solutions are another problem.
For example, an error variance may become negative or an estimate may have an unreasonable value.
This can happen because of sampling problems, weak indicators, or incorrect model specification.
Researchers should investigate the reason instead of just ignoring it.

# One-Step Versus Two-Step Modeling Approaches

In a one-step approach, the measurement model and structural model are estimated together.
This can save some time, but it is harder to know where the problem comes from when the model fit is poor.

In the two-step approach, researchers first estimate and evaluate the measurement model.
After the measurement model is acceptable, they estimate the structural model.
This makes it easier to separate a problem with the indicators from a problem with the theory.

The two-step approach also helps reduce interpretational confounding.
This problem happens when the meaning of a construct changes depending on which structural model is being tested.
By checking the measurement model first, the researcher can understand the constructs more clearly.

# The Confirmatory Structural Model

The structural model shows the expected relationships among the latent constructs.
It can include predictor constructs and outcome constructs.
The model is based on the theory that the researcher wants to test.

The structural model should be interpreted only after the measurement model has acceptable fit and validity.
If the indicators do not measure the constructs correctly, a significant path can be misleading.
Also, a good model fit does not prove that the theory is completely true.

Researchers need to be careful about causal language.
If the data is cross-sectional and correlational, it cannot by itself prove that one construct causes another construct.
Other factors may explain the relationship too.

# Recommended Two-Step Modeling Approach

The article's process can be summarized in these steps:

1\.
Make a measurement model based on the theory and past research.

2\.
Check if the indicators are measuring the constructs in a good way.

3.
Make changes only when there is a clear reason for it.

4\.
After that, test and compare the structural models.

The authors also discuss nested models and chi-square difference tests.
These tests help researchers compare the structural models.
The models should still make sense with the theory, not only fit the data.

# Advantages of the Two-Step Approach

-   It helps separate measurement problems from structural problems.

-    It shows if the indicators are measuring the constructs in a good way.

-   It makes it easier to compare different theory models.

# Additional Considerations in Structural Model Interpretation

Researchers should not treat SEM results as automatic proof of causality.
A significant path can be consistent with a causal theory, but correlation by itself does not prove cause and effect.

Researchers should also think about other possible explanations and alternative models.
One model can fit the data, but another model may fit it too.
The preferred model should be supported by theory, measurement quality, and comparison with other reasonable models.

For a Salesforce adoption project, a relationship between Salesforce usage and data quality should not immediately be called a causal relationship.
Employee role, training, manager support, and workflow differences could also affect the results.
These possible factors should be considered in the analysis.

# Conclusion

The main contribution of this article is giving researchers a practical way to use SEM more carefully.
Researchers should first check if their constructs are measured in a valid and clear way.
After that, they can test the relationships between the constructs.

The two-step approach makes it easier to understand where a model problem may come from.
It also makes the conclusions more believable.
The most important lesson for me is that measurement should be checked before researchers explain the structural relationships.

# References

Anderson, James C., and David W. Gerbing.
1988.
“Structural Equation Modeling in Practice: A Review and Recommended Two-Step Approach.” *Psychological Bulletin* 103 (3): 411–423.
https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.103.3.411.
